bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "California State Motor Vehicle and Engine Pollution Control Standards; Advanced Clean Cars II; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision".
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
subjects: Hybrid, electric, and advanced technology vehicles
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution nullifies the Environmental Protection Agency notice titled California State Motor Vehicle and Engine Pollution Control Standards; Advanced Clean Cars II; Waiver of Preemption; Notice of Decision (90 Fed. Reg. 642) and published on January 6, 2025. Among other elements, the notice grants the California Air Resources Board request for a waiver for its Advanced Clean Cars II (ACC II) regulations. (Under the Clean Air Act, California may seek waivers of the preemption prohibiting states from enacting certain emission standards.)

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn an Environmental Protection Agency decision that allowed California to enforce its Advanced Clean Cars II regulations. Those regulations set emission standards for vehicles sold in California that differ from federal standards. If passed, the resolution would nullify the waiver that permits California to apply its own rules.

industries.rationale: Automotive manufacturers would face different regulatory obligations depending on whether California's distinct emission standards remain in effect.
The Advanced Clean Cars II regulations affect the market for electric vehicle charging infrastructure and clean-energy vehicle adoption.
Electric utilities face demand changes tied to electric vehicle adoption rates influenced by state emission standards.
Petroleum refiners and distributors face market impacts from regulations that affect the mix of gasoline versus electric vehicles sold.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
